units.translation: Always is the fear of women excessive.
And a deep stain of misfortune always turns me back.
Always guarding the station over the fire.
Ares always loves all the best things of men (the sense requires "to hunt" or something similar) of the army.
For if his target is always my head,
And always he will dwell apart in hatred.
Flatter the one in power always,
I am always with many nightly dreams.
To guide the same fortune always.
May the fate that always brings endless sleep come upon us.
Having gone always over the earth trodden by wanderers.
They always honor this city of Pallas.
Always greatly honoring the kindly ones.
And we pray that other tributes of the earth may always be born.
And may they always honor the gods who hold the land.
Who always (αἰέν M) crosses through Acheron.
Where the all-seeing Sun always rests.
And even here always (i.e. always up to now) I do not blame this small thing.
Having sacrifices, you will praise this word forever.
Always groaning, bearing the mighty strength that is supreme.
And of the olive that always flourishes in its leaves, equal to...
Weeping, always neglecting the torch-bearing, and in dreams
he uses the ancient Attic form as much as possible, when he writes the diphthong αι instead of α, saying αἰεί
the one in power at any given time
the oar-stroke, which always crosses through Acheron
But when I think to sing or to warble.
Who then prevailed upon the bridegrooms to sing (the wedding song).

Concerning which plant see Athenaeus 14 p. 679a and 7 p. 296 f. With the less Attic form άειζώου, which Aeschylus used for metrical reasons, compare φιλόζωος [fond of life], which Sophocles (fr. 807) undoubtedly said for the same reason instead of φιλόζως [fond of life]. The Attic form ἀείζων [ever-living] was noted by Phrynichus in Bekker's Anecdota p. 22.
He who eats the ever-living, imperishable grass
And I somehow taste of the ever-living grass.
And may the land be an ever-living burden.
The disyllabic form αἰκης, which Sophocles also used,
Bekker's Anecdota p. 347,33: ἄειλα [shady places]: the very shady places, from the privation of ἕλη [sunlight] (εἵλη in Hesychius and in the Etymologicum M.) thus Aeschylus.
ἄειλα: the very shady places, from the privation of ἕλη (εἵλη)
a deed – greatest, ever to be remembered,
[perpetual host. Uncertain conjecture of Schneider at Ch. 684 for ἀεὶ ξένον.]
And another wave lifts a triple-crested one.
Lifting the saffron-dyed sandal of his foot.
